title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Problem 80: describe the residues of fourth powers modulo a prime P. Euler takes a primitive root a, so the fourth-power residues are the classes a^{4k}.

Case II, P = 4n+3. Here gcd(4, P-1) = 2. The powers a^{4k} for k = 0..2n reduce, via a^{4n+2} ≡ 1, to every even power a^{2j}. Every even power is a square, so the fourth-power residues are exactly the quadratic residues. In modern terms, x -> x^2 is a bijection on the squares when P ≡ 3 mod 4.

Coroll. 1 (§81), P = 4n+1. The fourth-power residues form the subgroup of index 4, with n elements. Each one is hit by exactly four bases p, q, r, s in [1, P-1]. These satisfy s ≡ -p and r ≡ -q, and in fact {p, q, r, s} = {p·ζ^k} with ζ of order 4. Euler concludes that p+q+r+s, p²+q²+r²+s² and p³+q³+r³+s³ are all ≡ 0 mod P. In modern terms, the roots of X^4 - c have e1 = e2 = e3 = 0, so by Newton's identities the power sums s1, s2, s3 vanish.

Coroll. 2 (§82). The solutions of x^4 ≡ 1 are 1, b, b², b³, where b is any solution other than 1; since b^4 ≡ 1 the list closes.

Coroll. 3 (§83, continued on the next page). Since a^{2n} ≡ -1, the class -1 is a fourth-power residue iff 4 | 2n, i.e. iff n is even, i.e. iff P ≡ 1 mod 8. In that case the residues are closed under negation. If P ≡ 5 mod 8, then -1 is a quartic non-residue.

The whole page serves the later scholion: for P = 8m+1 there is a sum of two fourth powers b⁴ + p⁴ divisible by P. This gives ±2 as quadratic residues, leading to Fermat's theorem that P = x² + 2y².
errors: Gap in Coroll. 1: from s ≡ -p and r ≡ -q alone, the sums of first and third powers vanish trivially. The sum of squares becomes 2(p² + q²), and its vanishing needs q² ≡ -p². That holds because q⁴ ≡ p⁴ while q² ≢ p² (otherwise q ≡ ±p), but Euler does not say so. The claim is correct; only the justification is left implicit.

In Case II the interpolated progression 1, a², a⁴, ..., a^{8n} overshoots. The distinct residues already end at a^{4n}, so the extra terms repeat earlier residues. This is harmless redundancy, not an error.

ideas.what: For p ≡ 3 mod 4, fourth-power residues coincide with quadratic residues
ideas.modern_name: Power residues of order gcd(k, p-1); the image of x -> x^k equals the image of x -> x^{gcd(k, p-1)}
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (residue theory via primitive roots); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), §§ on power residues
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 18, 1774); also Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792, posthumous)

ideas.what: For p ≡ 1 mod 4 there are (p-1)/4 quartic residues, each with four roots ±p, ±q
ideas.modern_name: Index-4 subgroup of (Z/p)^*; fourth roots of a residue differ by fourth roots of unity

ideas.what: Power sums p^k + q^k + r^k + s^k ≡ 0 mod P for k = 1, 2, 3 over the four roots of x⁴ ≡ c
ideas.modern_name: Vanishing of power sums of the roots of X⁴ - c (Newton's identities; sums of roots of unity)

ideas.what: -1 is a quartic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 8

deep.surprise_reason: Standard elementary results on quartic residues obtained with primitive roots, in a published 1774 paper that is well known in histories of quadratic and quartic residues (e.g. Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History). The power-sum remark is a minor, routine observation.
transcription_corrections: The final exponent in the interpolated progression is hard to read in the scan ('a^{8n}' versus a possible 'a^{4n}'). Logically a^{4n} suffices, but a^{8n} continues the previous page's progression; keep it as printed but flag it as uncertain.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image (long s rendered as s, 'vnde', 'diuisore', etc.).
